questions.stem: A product marketing lead runs all launch work in one Claude Project. In the first chat of the week, the team agreed the launch tagline and the three approved product claims. Two days later, in a new chat in the same Project, Claude drafts a landing page using a different tagline and an unapproved claim. The lead wants every future chat in the Project to start from the agreed decisions with the least ongoing effort. What should the lead do?

options.text: Ask Claude in each new chat to scroll back and reuse whatever the team agreed in the earlier launch chat.
Keep working in the original chat for all launch tasks so the agreed tagline always stays in view.
Add a short, dated 'Launch decisions' document with the tagline and approved claims to the Project knowledge.
Switch the Project to a more capable model so it can better infer what the team decided earlier.

questions.explanation: Chats in a Project each keep their own conversation history: a new chat does not see what was agreed in an earlier one. What every chat in a Project shares is the Project's knowledge. A short, dated 'Launch decisions' document means every new chat starts from the agreed tagline and claims, and there is one place to update when a decision changes.

whyWrong.A: A new chat cannot see another chat's history, so asking it to 'reuse' earlier decisions invites Claude to guess — and it depends on someone remembering to ask every time.
whyWrong.B: One endless chat gets long and cluttered, and colleagues starting their own chats still won't see the decisions. It works around the Project instead of using it.
whyWrong.D: A more capable model still cannot see a conversation it was never given. This is a missing-context problem, not a capability problem.

questions.mindset: If every chat must know it, it belongs in the Project knowledge, not in one chat's history.

questions.stem: An operations analyst sets up a Project to help the purchasing team answer supplier questions. To be thorough, she pasted the full 40-page supplier catalogue, the returns policy and her tone guidance into the project instructions box. Answers now often ignore the tone guidance and sometimes mix up catalogue details. Which change to the setup is MOST likely to improve results?

options.text: Move the catalogue and returns policy into project knowledge, and keep the instructions to a short brief on role, tone and file use.
Keep everything in the instructions but repeat the tone guidance at both the top and the bottom so it is harder for Claude to miss.
Split the catalogue into several smaller Projects, one per supplier, each with its own copy of the tone guidance in the instructions.
Leave the setup as it is and ask users to paste the relevant catalogue page into each chat before asking their question.

questions.explanation: Project instructions are for behaviour: who Claude helps, tone, format and rules. Project knowledge is for reference material. Burying a short tone rule inside 40 pages of catalogue text makes it easy to lose. Moving the reference documents into knowledge and keeping a short brief that points to them ("for returns questions, use the Returns Policy") gives Claude a clear set of rules and clearly separated sources.

whyWrong.B: Repeating a rule is a wording tweak. It doesn't fix the real problem, which is reference material sitting in the place meant for standing rules.
whyWrong.C: Splitting into many Projects is over-engineering. It multiplies the setups to maintain and copies the same guidance into each of them, while one well-organised Project would do.
whyWrong.D: Pasting material into every chat is the repetitive work a Project exists to remove, and it still leaves the cluttered instructions in place.

questions.mindset: Instructions carry behaviour; knowledge carries facts. Don't mix them.

questions.stem: An independent consultant uses Claude every week for two clients who compete in the same market. Each client has supplied confidential strategy documents. She wants Claude to help with each engagement while keeping the two sets of material, and anything Claude learns along the way, firmly apart. What is the BEST setup?

options.text: Use one Project for both clients and write an instruction telling Claude never to mention one client while working for the other.
Upload both clients' documents to one Project and name each file with the client's name so Claude can tell them apart.
Avoid Projects altogether and upload the relevant client's documents into ordinary chats each time she starts new work.
Create a separate Project for each client, each with its own instructions and only that client's knowledge files.

questions.explanation: Each Project is its own workspace: its own chats, its own knowledge base and, where memory is turned on, its own memory kept within that Project. A separate Project per client gives a clean boundary by design. An instruction or a file-naming convention only asks Claude to keep things apart; with both clients' files in one place, the material still sits in a single shared pool.

whyWrong.A: An instruction is guidance, not a boundary. Both clients' confidential files would still be in the same workspace and available to every chat in it.
whyWrong.B: Clear file names help, but they don't separate anything. Every chat can still draw on both clients' material.
whyWrong.C: Uploading files again for every new session is repetitive and error-prone. It is easy to attach the wrong client's file, and she gives up the reuse a Project offers.

questions.mindset: Separate bodies of work, especially confidential ones, get separate Projects.

questions.stem: A sales enablement manager on a Team plan has built a 'Deal Desk Q&A' Project with carefully curated pricing rules and approved discount guidance. Forty account executives need to use it every day. Two enablement leads are responsible for keeping its instructions and files accurate. Which TWO sharing decisions best protect the Project's accuracy while still giving everyone the access they need? Choose TWO.

options.text: Give all forty account executives 'Can edit' access so anyone can fix an error the moment they notice it.
Give the account executives 'Can view' access so they can chat with the Project but not change its setup.
Avoid sharing and ask each account executive to build a personal copy of the Project with the same files.
Share the Project with the whole organisation with edit rights so new hires are included automatically.
Give the two enablement leads 'Can edit' access so they own the instructions and knowledge files.

questions.explanation: Sharing a Project separates two abilities: using it (chatting with the Project and its knowledge) and editing it (changing its instructions and files). 'Can view' members can chat with the Project; 'Can edit' members can also change its contents. Giving edit rights only to the two people accountable for accuracy, and view rights to the forty who just need answers, keeps the curated pricing guidance under control while everyone gets full use of the Project.

whyWrong.A: Forty editors means nobody owns accuracy. Well-meant quick fixes pile up, conflict and quietly change the pricing guidance.
whyWrong.C: Forty personal copies drift apart the moment one is updated. It multiplies maintenance and defeats the point of a single curated source.
whyWrong.D: Organisation-wide sharing may be fine for viewing, but granting edit rights to everyone has the same ownership problem as option A, only bigger.

questions.mindset: Edit for the owners, view for the users.

questions.stem: A nonprofit development officer is setting up a Project to help draft grant applications for one major funder. She has access to the team's entire shared drive, which includes years of material. She wants the knowledge base to give reliable, on-brief drafts. Which TWO items should she add to project knowledge? Choose TWO.

options.text: The funder's current application guidelines and scoring criteria, published for this funding round.
Every past application the nonprofit has written to any funder, so Claude sees as much writing as possible.
The funder's guidelines from the three previous rounds, so Claude can compare how requirements have changed.
A recent successful application to this funder, clearly labelled as an example of structure and tone.
Internal draft versions with reviewers' tracked comments, so Claude can learn from past feedback.

questions.explanation: Good project knowledge is relevant, current and authoritative. The current guidelines tell Claude what this round requires. One clearly labelled successful application shows the structure and tone that worked with this funder. Extra material mostly adds noise and contradictions, and older guidelines can lead Claude to follow requirements that no longer apply.

whyWrong.B: Applications to other funders follow different rules and formats. More volume means more irrelevant and conflicting material, not better drafts.
whyWrong.C: Previous rounds' guidelines conflict with the current ones. Claude may follow an outdated requirement, and nothing in the answer will tell her it has.
whyWrong.E: Unfinished drafts with comments mix rejected wording with approved wording. They are not authoritative and can pull drafts in the wrong direction.

questions.mindset: Curate knowledge: current, relevant, authoritative. Volume is not quality.

questions.stem: A facilities coordinator has just finished configuring a Project that answers staff questions about booking meeting rooms and requesting equipment. Before announcing it to 300 colleagues, she wants confidence that it behaves as intended. What is the MOST effective next step?

options.text: Ask Claude in the Project to review its own instructions and confirm they are clear and complete.
Ask a handful of real questions with known answers, including one the documents don't cover, and check each reply.
Launch it to all staff straight away and rely on colleagues to report any answers that look wrong.
Add more documents to the knowledge base first, so the Project can handle any question staff might ask.

questions.explanation: A small test set with known correct answers shows directly whether Claude follows the instructions and uses the right document. Including a question the documents don't cover checks the most important failure case: whether Claude says it doesn't know or invents an answer. This is quick, cheap and catches problems before 300 people rely on it.

whyWrong.A: Asking Claude to judge its own setup is not evidence of how it answers real questions. Self-review is not a reliable check.
whyWrong.C: Using staff as testers means wrong answers reach people, and some will act on them, before anyone notices. Testing belongs before launch.
whyWrong.D: Adding material before testing anything makes problems harder to find and can bring in irrelevant or conflicting content.

questions.mindset: Test with known answers, including one it shouldn't answer, before anyone relies on it.

questions.stem: A global HR team's Project contains the company-wide Travel Policy and a UK Travel Addendum. Where the two differ, the addendum applies to UK-based staff. UK employees report that Claude sometimes quotes the global per-diem rate instead of the UK rate, while answers for other countries are correct. Both files are current. What is the MOST effective change with minimal disruption?

options.text: Delete the global Travel Policy from the Project, since UK staff are the ones reporting problems.
Merge both documents into one long file so Claude always reads the global and UK rules together.
Add a project instruction in capitals stating that the UK per-diem rate is always the correct one.
Add a project instruction saying the UK Addendum overrides the global policy for UK-based staff where they differ.

questions.explanation: Both files are correct and both are needed. What is missing is a rule for which one takes priority. One instruction that states the precedence ("for UK-based staff, the UK Travel Addendum overrides the global policy where they differ") gives Claude a clear tie-breaker that covers per-diems and every other difference.

whyWrong.A: Removing the global policy breaks answers for every other country and for any topic the addendum doesn't cover.
whyWrong.B: Merging doesn't say which rule wins. It creates a large file to maintain and hides where one document ends and the other begins.
whyWrong.C: This patches one symptom. It would wrongly apply the UK rate to non-UK staff and does nothing for the other topics where the two documents differ.

questions.mindset: When two valid sources overlap, state the precedence rule. Don't delete or shout.

questions.stem: A legal operations team loaded every contract document they could find into one Project: current contract templates, archived templates, duplicate copies with different filenames, and a single 300-page compiled PDF of every clause variation. The Project still answers, but it often pulls clauses from irrelevant or archived material. Which TWO actions are MOST likely to improve answer quality? Choose TWO.

options.text: Switch to the most capable model so it can work out on its own which of the documents matter.
Paste the five most-used templates into the project instructions so they are always read first.
Remove archived templates and duplicate copies so only the current, authoritative versions remain.
Add a project instruction asking Claude to double-check that each clause comes from a current template.
Replace the 300-page compiled PDF with clearly titled, separate documents organised by clause type.

questions.explanation: The setup, not the model, is the problem. Archived and duplicate templates put wrong passages right next to right ones, and the more material Claude has to work through, the more accuracy and recall suffer — capacity is no substitute for curation. Removing archived and duplicate files leaves only current, authoritative versions to draw on, and replacing the giant compiled PDF with clearly titled documents organised by clause type makes the right passages easy to find.

whyWrong.A: A bigger model can't fix a knowledge base full of stale and duplicate material. The wrong passages are still there to be drawn on.
whyWrong.B: Copying templates into the instructions creates a second copy of the content to maintain, bloats the instructions and leaves the clutter in place.
whyWrong.D: Asking Claude to double-check can't tell it which documents are archived and which are current. The fix is to remove what shouldn't be used.

questions.mindset: A knowledge base is only as good as what's in it: clean, current, well-organised files beat volume.

questions.stem: A retail planner added the team's 'Store Rollout Plan' Google Doc to a Project from Google Drive. Claude answers questions about dates and owners correctly, but says it can't find the opening budget for each region. The budget figures are in the document, but only as a screenshot of a spreadsheet pasted into the doc. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Replace the screenshot with a text table of the figures, or add the source sheet as a separate knowledge file.
Add a project instruction telling Claude to examine every image in the Rollout Plan carefully for budget figures.
Remove the doc and add it again from Google Drive so the Project picks up a fresh copy of its contents.
Give Claude edit access to the Google Doc so it can open the embedded screenshot at full resolution.

questions.explanation: When Claude reads a Google Drive file, it extracts the text content; images embedded in the document are not processed. The doc already reflects its current version, so the problem is not staleness: the figures are simply not in a form Claude reads. Putting them in as text (or adding the actual spreadsheet as its own source) makes them available.

whyWrong.B: No instruction can make Claude read content it doesn't receive. Embedded images in Drive documents aren't processed, however the request is worded.
whyWrong.C: Re-adding the same doc from Drive doesn't change what's in it. The figures would still be locked inside an image.
whyWrong.D: Access level isn't the issue. Claude can already read the doc's text. The figures just aren't text.

questions.mindset: Diagnose why the answer is missing before reaching for wording or access fixes.

questions.stem: A customer education team uses a Project to draft help-centre articles. They want Claude to use the uploaded product guides as the main source, but also to add general best-practice tips from its own knowledge where useful. Reviewers say they can't tell which statements come from the product guides and which are Claude's general advice, so checking takes too long. What is the BEST change to the project configuration?

options.text: Remove the product guides so every article is written from general knowledge and is reviewed the same way.
Add an instruction forbidding any content that is not in the product guides, including general best-practice tips.
Add an instruction to mark which statements come from a named product guide and which are general advice.
Ask Claude, at the end of each draft, to rate how confident it is in the overall accuracy of the article.

questions.explanation: The team wants both kinds of content. The problem is that reviewers can't tell them apart. An instruction to label or cite which guide each product statement comes from, and to mark general advice as such, keeps the useful tips and lets reviewers focus their checking on the product claims.

whyWrong.A: Removing the authoritative source makes every product claim harder to check and more likely to be wrong.
whyWrong.B: This throws away tips the team explicitly wants. It solves the review problem by removing value instead of making the content checkable.
whyWrong.D: A self-rated confidence score is not a reliable accuracy signal, and it doesn't tell reviewers which statements to check against the guides.

questions.mindset: Configure for the review step: make the source of each claim visible.

questions.stem: An events manager is setting up a Project for the annual partner conference. She has the signed venue contract, the catering menu and price list, and her team's working rules: every proposal must show costs in euros, flag any deposit deadline in the next 30 days, and be written for non-specialist partners. Which configuration is BEST?

options.text: Put the contract, menu and the three working rules all in project knowledge, and leave the instructions blank.
Put the contract and menu in project knowledge, and the three working rules in the project instructions.
Put the three working rules in her account-wide instructions, and upload the contract and menu to each chat.
Paste the contract and menu text into the project instructions, and save the working rules as a knowledge file.

questions.explanation: Reference material (the contract and price list) belongs in project knowledge, where every chat in the Project can draw on it. Rules about how every response should look (currency, deadline flags, audience) are standing behaviour, so they belong in the project instructions, which shape every chat in that Project.

whyWrong.A: Rules saved as a knowledge file are treated as background to look things up in, not as directions for every response. They may be followed inconsistently.
whyWrong.C: Account-wide instructions apply to all of her chats, including unrelated ones, and uploading files to each chat brings back the repetition a Project removes.
whyWrong.D: This is backwards: long reference text crowds the instructions, and the behaviour rules end up treated as background reading.

questions.mindset: Rules shape every answer → instructions. Facts to look up → knowledge.

questions.stem: A finance business partner's 'Monthly Commentary' Project holds this month's results spreadsheet plus two approved past commentaries that show the house structure and tone. Drafts follow the right structure, but sometimes repeat revenue figures and explanations from the old commentaries instead of this month's data. Which TWO changes are MOST effective? Choose TWO.

options.text: Add an instruction that the commentaries are format examples only, and every figure must come from the current results file.
Remove the past commentaries entirely, so the only file Claude can see is this month's results spreadsheet.
Rename the example files with clear labels, for example 'FORMAT EXAMPLE – figures out of date', so their role is obvious.
Switch to a more capable model so it can work out for itself which of the numbers belong to this month's results.
Ask Claude to re-read its finished draft and confirm that all the numbers in it look reasonable before sending it out.

questions.explanation: Examples are a powerful way to show structure and tone, but Claude can treat their content as source material unless the role of each file is clear. Saying in the instructions that the examples are for format only, with figures taken from the current results file, and labelling the example files the same way, keeps the benefit of the examples and removes the confusion.

whyWrong.B: Removing the examples entirely fixes the figures but loses the structure and tone they were added for. It throws out what works.
whyWrong.D: A more capable model still sees two sets of plausible numbers with no rule about which to use. The fix is to make the role of each file clear.
whyWrong.E: An old figure can look perfectly 'reasonable' in a finished draft. A self-check doesn't tell Claude which source is current.

questions.mindset: Tell Claude what each knowledge file is for, especially examples.

questions.stem: A school administrator needs to translate a single parent letter about a one-off schedule change into Spanish today. A colleague suggests first building a dedicated Claude Project with translation instructions and the school's style guide. The administrator has no other translation work planned. What is the MOST appropriate approach?

options.text: Build the Project as suggested, because Projects always give more accurate results than ordinary chats.
Build the Project and share it with the whole school in case anyone else needs a translation later.
Use an ordinary chat with clear context about the audience and tone, then have a fluent speaker check it.
Upload the school's whole policy library to a new Project so the translation uses consistent terms.

questions.explanation: A Project pays off when the same context and rules are reused across many chats. For a single, one-off task, an ordinary chat with a clear brief is simpler and just as good. Because the letter goes to parents, a quick check by a fluent speaker is the right safeguard.

whyWrong.A: Projects add reuse and organisation, not automatic accuracy. Setting one up for a single task is unnecessary overhead.
whyWrong.B: Building and sharing a Project 'just in case' creates something nobody owns or maintains, for a need that doesn't exist yet.
whyWrong.D: Loading a whole policy library for one letter adds irrelevant material and effort with no benefit.

questions.mindset: Match the tool to the task: Projects are for repeated work.

questions.stem: An IT service desk lead built a Project to answer staff questions about the new password policy. To give Claude 'full context', she uploaded the 90-minute transcript of the steering meeting where the policy was debated, and no other document. Claude now sometimes tells staff that passwords expire every 60 days, which was one option discussed but rejected. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Add an instruction telling Claude to ignore any opinions expressed in the meeting transcript.
Keep the transcript and add an instruction stating the correct expiry period in bold capital letters.
Ask staff to double-check every answer against the transcript before acting on what Claude says.
Replace the transcript with the final approved policy document as the Project's knowledge source.

questions.explanation: Claude treats project knowledge as trustworthy background. A transcript of a debate contains rejected options alongside the final decision, so it is not an authoritative source. The fix is to use the approved policy document, the single source of truth, as the knowledge.

whyWrong.A: Claude can't reliably tell which statements in a long debate were opinions and which became policy. The confusing source stays in place.
whyWrong.B: This patches one fact while every other rejected option in the transcript can still turn up in answers.
whyWrong.C: This pushes the burden onto every user and makes them check against the same confusing source that caused the error.

questions.mindset: Knowledge should be the authoritative record, not the discussion that led to it.

questions.stem: On an Enterprise plan, a people analytics lead has used a private Project for six months to prepare manager guidance. Leadership now wants the Project shared with the broader organisation so every manager can use it. The knowledge base has grown over time and the lead isn't sure everything in it is still appropriate. What should the lead do BEFORE changing the sharing setting?

options.text: Review every knowledge file and remove anything not suitable for all managers to see, such as named salary data.
Share it organisation-wide now and add an instruction telling Claude never to reveal any confidential file contents.
Share it organisation-wide with view-only access, since view-only members cannot reach the knowledge files.
Duplicate the instructions into a new Project with no knowledge, and share that empty version instead.

questions.explanation: When a Project is shared with the broader organisation, everyone in it can view and use the Project, and so can draw on its knowledge in their chats. A knowledge base that built up while the Project was private may hold material that was fine for one person but not for every manager. The right control is to curate the knowledge before widening access.

whyWrong.B: An instruction is not an access control. Confidential material in the knowledge base can still surface in answers.
whyWrong.C: View-only stops people changing the setup. It does not stop them using the Project, and its knowledge, in their chats.
whyWrong.D: Removing all knowledge throws away the useful guidance leadership wants shared. Curating it is the proportionate step.

questions.mindset: Widening who can use a Project widens who can reach its knowledge. Curate first.
